title: Judaism: beliefs and practices

explain.say: Judaism is one of the oldest religions that worship one God, with roots more than 3,000 years old in the land of Israel. Today there are about 15 million Jews, most of them in Israel and the United States.

draw.label: Places in the Torah story: Abraham from Ur, the Torah at Sinai, Jerusalem

explain.say: Jews believe God made a covenant, a special promise, with Abraham, and later gave the Torah to Moses at Mount Sinai. The Ten Commandments are at its heart.

draw.text: Covenant: a binding promise between God and the Jewish people

explain.say: The central prayer, the Shema, declares that God is one. The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, the Tanakh, and the rabbis' discussions of it fill the Talmud.

items: Torah: the five books of Moses

draw.text: The Shema: Hear, O Israel: the Lord is our God, the Lord is one. (Deuteronomy 6:4)

explain.say: Every week Jews keep Shabbat, a day of rest from Friday at sunset to Saturday night. Families light candles, bless wine and challah bread, share a meal and many attend the synagogue.

items: Challah bread and a family meal

explain.say: Jews today practise in many ways. Orthodox Jews keep the traditional laws closely, Conservative Jews balance tradition and change, and Reform Jews adapt practice to modern life.

faq.a: Shabbat is the Jewish day of rest, from sunset on Friday to nightfall on Saturday. It remembers that God rested on the seventh day of creation. Families light candles, share a meal, pray and rest from work.
asks: What is the Sabbath in Judaism?
Why do Jews rest on Saturday?

faq.a: The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. Jews believe God gave it to Moses. In the synagogue it is handwritten on a scroll and read aloud every week.
asks: What is the Jewish holy book?

faq.a: Jews believe in one God who created the world and made a covenant with the Jewish people, through Abraham and Moses. They try to live by God's commandments in the Torah, through prayer, study, justice and kindness.

A synagogue is a place for prayer, study and community. Services include prayers, often in Hebrew, and readings from the Torah scroll, which is kept in a cabinet called the Ark. A rabbi teaches and guides the community.

faq.q: What is the covenant in Judaism?
faq.a: The covenant is a special agreement between God and the Jewish people. The Torah tells that God promised Abraham his descendants would become a great people, and at Sinai the people agreed to keep God's laws.
asks: What promise did God make to Abraham?

faq.a: Kosher means fit or proper food under Jewish law. Kosher rules forbid pork and shellfish, require animals to be slaughtered in a set way, and keep meat and dairy apart. Many Jews keep kosher, some strictly and some partly.
asks: Why do Jews not eat pork?

faq.a: Passover, or Pesach, remembers how the Israelites were freed from slavery in Egypt, led by Moses. Families hold a special meal called the seder, retell the story, and eat matzah, flat bread made without yeast.

Hanukkah is the eight-day festival of lights. It remembers the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem over 2,000 years ago, when, as tradition tells, a little oil burned for eight days. Families light one more candle each night on a hanukkiah.
asks: Why do Jews light eight candles?
What is the festival of lights in Judaism?

faq.a: Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, is the holiest day of the Jewish year. Many Jews fast for about 25 hours and spend the day in prayer, asking forgiveness from God and from people they have wronged.
asks: What is the Day of Atonement?
Why do Jews fast on Yom Kippur?

faq.q: What is a bar mitzvah or bat mitzvah?
faq.a: It is the coming of age when a Jewish child becomes responsible for keeping the commandments: 13 for boys, and 12 or 13 for girls. Many celebrate by reading from the Torah in the synagogue, followed by a party.
asks: What happens at a bar mitzvah?

faq.q: What are the different types of Judaism?
faq.a: The main movements are Orthodox, which keeps traditional law closely, Conservative, in between, and Reform, which adapts practice to modern life. There are also Reconstructionist and secular Jews. Each sees itself as faithful to Judaism.

faq.q: Why do Jewish men wear a kippah?
faq.a: A kippah, or yarmulke, is a small cap worn as a sign of respect and awareness that God is above. Orthodox men wear one all the time; others wear it for prayer. In some communities women wear one too.
asks: Why do Jews cover their heads?

faq.q: What is the Star of David?
faq.a: The Star of David, a six-pointed star, is a widely known symbol of Judaism and the Jewish people, and appears on the flag of Israel. The menorah, a seven-branched lampstand from the ancient Temple, is an even older symbol.

The Western Wall in Jerusalem is part of the wall that surrounded the ancient Temple compound, destroyed by the Romans in 70 CE. It is the holiest place where Jews pray today, and many tuck written prayers into its cracks.
asks: Why is the Western Wall important?

facts: Jews numbered about 14.8 million in 2020, about 0.2 percent of the world (Pew Research).
The Torah is the first five books of the Hebrew Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy.
Shabbat lasts from sunset on Friday to nightfall on Saturday.
The Tanakh is made of the Torah, the Nevi'im (Prophets) and the Ketuvim (Writings).
The Second Temple in Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans in 70 CE.
